title: Binary trees
objectives: Traverse a binary tree in pre-order, in-order and post-order.
Walk a tree level by level with a queue
Write traversals that handle the empty tree

screens.title: Nodes with nothing below
screens.prose:
A binary tree stores values in **nodes**. Each node holds a value and two links, `left` and `right`. A link to nothing is `None`.

```python
class Node:
    def __init__(self, val):
        self.val = val
        self.left = None
        self.right = None
```

state.caption: The top node, A, is the **root**.

screens.question: Tap every node whose `left` and `right` are both `None`.

hints.text: Look for the nodes with no line going down from them.
B has two lines going down, to D and E.
D, E, F and G have nothing below them.

feedback.correct: D, E, F and G have no children.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Tap only the nodes with no lines going down from them.

byKey.l: B links to D and E, so its `left` and `right` are not `None`.
byKey.r: C links to F and G, so its `left` and `right` are not `None`.

explain.text: A node with no children is a **leaf**: D, E, F and G. A, B and C each have two children. Every node except the root has exactly one parent.

canvas.caption: Leaves: D, E, F and G. Root: A.

screens.title: How far down
screens.prose: A program holding only `root` reaches G by following links: `root.right`, then `.right` again.
screens.question: How many links does it follow from A to G?

hints.text: Count the lines, not the nodes.
The path runs A to C, then C to G.
Two lines: A to C and C to G.

feedback.correct: Two links: A to C, then C to G.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the lines on the path from A to G.

byKey.nodes: You counted the nodes A, C and G. Count the links between them instead: there are two.

explain.text: The links from the root down to a node give its **depth**: G has depth 2, A has depth 0. The greatest depth, 2 here, is the tree's **height**. So a tree of one node has height 0.

canvas.caption: Depth of G: 2. Height of the tree: 2.

screens.title: Print, then go left
screens.prose:
This function walks the whole tree. We call `visit(root)`.

```python
def visit(node):
    if node is None:
        return
    print(node.val)
    visit(node.left)
    visit(node.right)
```
screens.question: Put the letters in the order it prints them.

hints.text: The first call prints A before anything else.
After A, `visit(node.left)` must finish the whole of B's side before C is reached.
A, then B, D, E, then C, F, G.

feedback.correct: A, B, D, E, C, F, G.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Follow the calls: print, then all of the left side, then the right side.

byKey.C: You printed C straight after B, level by level. The call on B finishes D and E before C is reached.
byKey.D: You printed D first. Here `print` runs before `visit(node.left)`, so A is printed first.

explain.text: Each call prints its node before either recursive call. So A comes first, then all of B's side, then all of C's side. This order is **pre-order**.

canvas.caption: Pre-order: A B D E C F G

screens.title: Left first
screens.prose:
Now `print` moves between the two calls.

```python
def visit(node):
    if node is None:
        return
    visit(node.left)
    print(node.val)
    visit(node.right)
```
screens.question: Put the letters in the order it prints them now.

hints.text: Before A is printed, `visit(node.left)` runs on B. Before B is printed, it runs on D.
D has no children, so it is printed first.
D, B, E, then A, then F, C, G.

feedback.correct: D, B, E, A, F, C, G.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each node is printed after its left side and before its right side.

byKey.A: You printed A first. `visit(node.left)` now runs before `print`, so the whole left side comes before A.
byKey.E: You printed E before B. B is printed between its left side, D, and its right side, E.

explain.text: Every node is printed after its left side and before its right side. So D, B, E fill the left, then A, then F, C, G. This is **in-order**.

canvas.caption: In-order: D B E A F C G

screens.title: Children first
screens.prose:
Now `print` comes after both calls.

```python
def visit(node):
    if node is None:
        return
    visit(node.left)
    visit(node.right)
    print(node.val)
```
screens.question: Put the letters in the order it prints them.

hints.text: A cannot be printed until both of its sides are finished.
B waits for D and E.
D, E, B, then F, G, C, and A last.

feedback.correct: D, E, B, F, G, C, A.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. A node is printed only after both its sides are done.

byKey.A: You printed A first. Both recursive calls now run before `print`, so A comes last.
byKey.B: You printed B between D and E. B waits for both of its children now.

explain.text: A node is printed only after both its sides are finished, so the root comes last. This is **post-order**. A parent waits for its children, which is what a calculation over the tree needs.

canvas.caption: Post-order: D E B F G C A

screens.title: Level by level
screens.prose:
To list the tree level by level we use a queue, as in level 3.

```python
def level_order(root):
    out = []
    q = deque([root] if root else [])
    while q:
        node = q.popleft()
        out.append(node.val)
        if node.left:
            q.append(node.left)
        if node.right:
            q.append(node.right)
    return out
```
screens.question: What does the queue hold just after C has been taken out and its children added?

options.why: You dropped D and E. They were added when B came out and are still waiting at the front.
You stopped before adding C's children. Taking C out adds F and G at the back.
You put C's children at the front. A queue adds at the back, so D and E stay ahead.

hints.text: Run the loop by hand: A comes out first.
A adds B and C. Then B comes out and adds D and E.
C comes out next and adds F and G behind D and E.

feedback.correct: D, E, F, G: the whole next level, in order.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Run the loop: take from the front, add children at the back.

explain.text: A comes out and adds B, C. B comes out and adds D, E. C comes out and adds F, G behind, so first in, first out keeps each level ahead of the next.

canvas.caption: Queue after C: D E F G. Output so far: A B C

screens.title: Three traversals in code
screens.prose: `Node`, `build` and `deque` are ready to use. `build` reads a level-order list, left to right. `None` marks a missing child, which gets no children of its own in the list.
screens.question: Write `preorder(root)`, `inorder(root)` and `level_order(root)`, each returning a list of values.

widget.how: Check runs 14 hidden tests and compares lists exactly. They include an empty tree (`None`), one node, and long chains.

hints.text: Start each recursive function with the empty tree: `if root is None: return []`.
In-order joins three lists: the left side's, `[root.val]`, then the right side's.
`return inorder(root.left) + [root.val] + inorder(root.right)`. Pre-order puts `[root.val]` first. Level order is the queue loop from the last screen.

feedback.correct: All three traversals pass, including the empty tree and the chains.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-2: Test 2 expects `[4, 2, 5, 1, 6, 3, 7]`. If 1 came first, you added the node before its left side.
byKey.test-5: Test 5 passes `None`, an empty tree. Start with `if root is None: return []`.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 passes an empty tree. Start the queue empty when `root` is `None`, or `node.val` fails.

explain.text: Each recursive version is an empty case plus two sides joined around the node. Only the place of `[root.val]` changes. Level order swaps the recursion for a queue.

screens.title: The node in the wrong place
screens.prose:
This is meant to return in-order. On the A to G tree it returns A, B, D, E, C, F, G.

```python
def inorder(node):
    if node is None:
        return []
    out = [node.val]
    out += inorder(node.left)
    out += inorder(node.right)
    return out
```

state.caption: Returned: A B D E C F G

screens.question: Which change makes it return D, B, E, A, F, C, G?

options.text: Add `node.val` after the left side, not before it

options.why: Swapping them gives A, C, G, F, B, E, D. The node still comes first; only the sides are mirrored.

options.text: Add a check `if node.left is None`
options.why: The `None` case is already handled at the top. The bug is where the node's own value goes.
Sorting gives A to G alphabetically. Tree positions are not alphabetical, so sorting only hides the bug.

hints.text: Which node does the function output first, and why?
A is added to `out` before the left side is visited.
In-order needs the left side, then the node, then the right side.

feedback.correct: The node must sit between its two sides.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at where `node.val` goes relative to the left side.

byKey.b: You swapped the calls, but the node is still added first. That is pre-order of the mirror image.
byKey.d: You sorted the output. That hides the bug on this tree and fails on any tree not labelled in order.

explain.text: Putting `node.val` first is pre-order, whatever the function is called. In-order is `inorder(node.left) + [node.val] + inorder(node.right)`. The other classic slip is dropping the `None` check: `None.left` raises `AttributeError`.

canvas.caption: In-order starts at D, the leftmost node

screens.title: One pattern, three orders
screens.prose:
We wrote three traversals with one pattern. Only the place of the node changes.

```python
def walk(node):
    if node is None:        # empty tree
        return []
    left = walk(node.left)
    right = walk(node.right)
    return [node.val] + left + right   # pre
    # left + [node.val] + right        # in
    # left + right + [node.val]        # post
```

Each node is visited once. Appending to one shared list keeps a walk $O(n)$.
screens.question: A parent needs its children's results before it can compute its own. Which order fits?

options.why: Pre-order handles the parent first, before its children have produced anything.
In-order handles the parent after its left child but before its right child, so one result is missing.
Level order reaches the parent before every node on the levels below it.

feedback.correct: Post-order finishes both children before the parent.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which order handles the node after both of its sides?

explain.text: Post-order runs both calls before using the node, so the children's results are ready. Sizes, heights and sums of subtrees all work this way. Lesson 16 is built on it.

screens.title: An expression tree for P&L
screens.prose: A risk system stores formulas as **expression trees**. Leaves hold numbers. Inner nodes hold operators and apply them to their two children, left first.

state.caption: P&L of 50 shares bought at £100, now £108, less a £12 fee

screens.question: Evaluate the tree. What is the P&L in £?

hints.text: Start at the bottom: an operator can work only once both its children are numbers.
The lowest operator is 108 − 100.
108 − 100 = 8, then 50 × 8 = 400, then subtract the fee.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work from the bottom up: 108 − 100 first.

byKey.fee: You stopped at the × node. The root still subtracts the £12 fee.
byKey.sign: You subtracted the wrong way round. Each operator takes its left child first: 400 − 12.
byKey.gross: You treated × as + or skipped the inner −. The inner node gives 8, and 50 × 8 = 400.

explain.text: Post-order: 108 − 100 = 8, then 50 × 8 = 400, then 400 − 12 = 388. Each operator waits for both children, which is why expressions are evaluated post-order.

screens.title: Evaluate any payoff
screens.prose: Now in code. Leaves hold numbers. Inner nodes hold `'+'`, `'-'`, `'*'` or `'max'`, and always have two children. `max` builds option payoffs: a call pays `max(S - K, 0)`.
screens.question: Write `evaluate(node)`: return the value of the tree under `node`.

widget.how: Check runs 8 hidden tests. `'-'` means left minus right. Test 6 is a bull call spread.

hints.text: A leaf has `left` and `right` both `None`: return its value.
Otherwise evaluate both children first, then apply the operator. That is post-order.
`a = evaluate(node.left)`, `b = evaluate(node.right)`, then return `a + b`, `a - b`, `a * b` or `max(a, b)` by `node.val`.

feedback.correct: Every payoff evaluates, from a single number to a spread.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the first failing test.

byKey.test-4: Test 4 is a single leaf, 42. A leaf has no children: return its value without recursing.
byKey.test-7: Test 7 expects −7 for 3 − 10. Subtract the right child from the left.

explain.text: Both children are evaluated before the operator, so this is post-order. Test 6 is `max(110 − 95, 0) − max(110 − 105, 0)`, which is 15 − 5 = 10.

ideas: A binary tree is nodes with `left` and `right` links. `None` marks a missing child, and the empty tree is `None` itself.
Pre-order, in-order and post-order are one recursion. Only the place of the node changes: before, between or after its two sides.
Level order takes nodes from the front of a queue and adds their children at the back.

formula.name: Three depth-first orders
formula.tex: \text{pre}: v, L, R \qquad \text{in}: L, v, R \qquad \text{post}: L, R, v
formula.note: $v$ is the node, $L$ and $R$ its left and right sides. Every node is visited once: $O(n)$.

summary.trap: Adding the node before its left side gives pre-order, not in-order. And without `if node is None` the walk crashes at the first leaf.

quiz.prose: `build([5, 4, None, 3])` is a chain: 5 at the root, its left child 4, and 4's left child 3.
quiz.question: What does `inorder` return?

options.why: That is pre-order. In-order finishes the left side first, so the deepest node comes first.
You put 4 before its own left child, 3. In-order puts each node after its left side.
The `None` case returns `[]`, so a missing child adds nothing and nothing fails.

feedback.correct: The deepest left node comes first.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. In-order: left side, node, right side.

explain.text: In-order on 5 finishes its left side, 4, first. In-order on 4 finishes 3 first. So 3, 4, 5.

quiz.prose: A trading rule is a decision tree. Inner nodes ask yes-or-no questions; leaves say buy, sell or hold. You print it like nested `if` statements: each question, then its whole yes-branch, then its no-branch.
quiz.question: Which traversal prints it that way?

options.why: Post-order prints the answers first and the opening question last.
In-order prints the yes-branch before the question that leads to it.
Level order prints all the second questions together, apart from their own branches.

feedback.correct: Node, then left side, then right side.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. The question comes before both of its branches.

explain.text: Pre-order prints a node, then its whole left side, then its whole right side. That is exactly a question followed by its yes-branch and then its no-branch.

quiz.prose: A fund holds regions, regions hold desks, desks hold books. The risk report lists the fund, then every region, then every desk, then every book.
quiz.question: What do you walk the hierarchy with?

options.text: A queue: take from the front, add children at the back

options.why: Pre-order goes all the way down the first region before starting the second region.

options.text: A stack: take the newest node first
options.why: A stack takes the newest node first, so it dives deep instead of finishing a level.
Post-order lists the books first and the fund last.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Which structure finishes one level before the next?

explain.text: A queue hands back nodes in the order they were added. Every region is added before any desk, so the report goes level by level.

quiz.prose: We count height in links, from the root down to the deepest node.
quiz.question: What is the height of a tree with one node?

feedback.correct: Zero: there are no links to follow.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count links, not nodes.

byKey.nodes: You counted the node itself. Height counts links, and a lone root has none.

explain.text: A single node is the root and the deepest node at once, with no links between. Its height is 0. Lesson 16 uses this convention.
